subject: Science
title: Adaptation and Evolution
duration: 12 lessons of 50 minutes, including assessment and review
purpose: Learning about variation and adaptation helps students explain why organisms are suited to different environments. It also helps them reason about how environmental change affects populations and why conservation decisions matter in Aotearoa New Zealand.
prior: Year 7 Cells and Organisation: organisms are made of cells. Earlier learning about reproduction: offspring inherit characteristics from parents. Check these foundations before introducing selection.
future: Year 10 Genetics: inherited variation provides a foundation for explaining inheritance. Later ecology learning builds on explanations of population change and environmental pressures.
knowledgeSummary: Individuals within a species vary. Inherited features can affect survival and reproductive success in a particular environment. Over generations, natural selection can change the frequency of inherited characteristics in a population.
practicesSummary: Compare observations, recognise patterns in variation, interpret population data and use evidence to construct causal explanations. Evaluate what a model of natural selection represents and where it is limited.
resources: Photographs of variation within one species; named New Zealand organism case studies; population data; simple selection-model materials; mini whiteboards; shared assessment and marking schedule.
assessment: End-of-unit assessment combining retrieval questions, interpretation of a population graph and an explanation of natural selection in an unfamiliar context. Department to confirm the final task and coverage.
descriptors: Use the agreed Junior Assessment Framework and the departmental marking schedule. Add the link to the final assessment criteria before teaching.
reporting: Department to confirm the agreed reporting route and how this assessment contributes to reporting.

focuses.title: Variation within a species
focuses.objectives:
Identify variation among individuals of the same species.
Distinguish inherited influences from environmental influences on characteristics.
focuses.priorities:
Numeracy: organise a supplied set of measurements and describe its distribution.
Literacy: use compare and whereas to describe differences precisely.
Capabilities: Thinkers — justify classifications using evidence.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: compare, classify, characteristic, evidence.
Tier 3: species, variation, inherited, environmental.
focuses.misconceptions:
All individuals of the same species are identical.
Every difference between individuals is inherited.
focuses.checks:
Mini whiteboards: classify examples of variation and justify one choice.
Hinge question: distinguish an inherited characteristic from a change caused by the environment.

focuses.title: Adaptations in different environments
focuses.objectives:
Identify structural, behavioural and physiological adaptations in named examples.
Explain how a particular feature supports survival or reproduction in a specified environment.
focuses.priorities:
Literacy: model a feature → effect → survival explanation.
Local context / place: apply the explanation to a named New Zealand organism using a reliable case study.
Capabilities: Communicators — explain a feature and respond to a partner’s challenge.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: function, advantage, explain, environment.
Tier 3: adaptation, structural, behavioural, physiological.
focuses.misconceptions:
A useful feature is equally advantageous in every environment.
An individual develops an inherited adaptation because it needs one.
focuses.checks:
Compare an example and non-example of an adaptation.
Exit ticket: explain how one named feature provides an advantage in its environment.

focuses.title: Natural selection across generations
focuses.objectives:
Explain how inherited variation, a selection pressure and differences in reproductive success can change a population over generations.
Interpret a graph showing a change in the frequency of a characteristic.
focuses.priorities:
Numeracy: compare proportions in population data over generations.
Literacy: construct a causal explanation using because, therefore and over generations.
Capabilities: Thinkers — evaluate the limitations of a selection model.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: proportion, pressure, consequence, generation.
Tier 3: natural selection, selection pressure, population, reproductive success.
focuses.misconceptions:
Individuals evolve during their lifetime.
Natural selection always favours the strongest organism.
All organisms survive equally well and pass on their characteristics equally often.
focuses.checks:
Hinge question: decide whether change occurs within an individual or across generations in a population.
Mini whiteboards: predict a population change after a stated environmental pressure and explain why.

focuses.title: Applying explanations to environmental change
focuses.objectives:
Use evidence to explain how environmental change can affect a population.
Apply natural selection to an unfamiliar organism and distinguish evidence from an unsupported claim.
focuses.priorities:
Literacy: justify a claim with relevant evidence and a scientific explanation.
Student futures: evaluate an environmental claim before making a conservation recommendation.
Capabilities: Reflective — improve an explanation after feedback.
focuses.vocabulary:
Tier 2: interpret, justify, evaluate, consequence.
Tier 3: evolution, selection pressure, population, adaptation.
focuses.misconceptions:
Environmental change always leads to a population successfully adapting.
A change in population size alone proves that evolution has occurred.
focuses.checks:
Short unfamiliar-context response: explain an observed population pattern using evidence.
Review a model answer and identify the causal link missing from a weaker response.
